subject: technology
unit_title: Digital Citizenship, Privacy, and Kindness Online
essential_question: How can understanding digital citizenship, privacy, and kindness online help us explain, decide, create, or solve something that matters?
standards: Michigan Computer Science: Impacts of Computing
Michigan Computer Science: Networks and the Internet
project_brief: Create a digital-safety guide for a younger learner using fictional examples and no real credentials. This is the grade 4 culminating project for "Digital Citizenship, Privacy, and Kindness Online" (ma-g4-tech-cs-u01, unit 1), built around digital footprints, evaluating a website for trust, strong practice passphrases, reporting unsafe or unkind content, and balancing screen time. Create the safety or citizenship artifact for this unit using only fictional names, fictional accounts, and invented examples — never real personal information, real screenshots of real accounts, or a real classmate's data.
requirements: Address every topic listed for this unit: digital footprints, evaluating a website for trust, strong practice passphrases, reporting unsafe or unkind content, balancing screen time, and respecting others' privacy online.
Meet the performance task as written: Create a digital-safety guide for a younger learner using fictional examples and no real credentials.
Show your work or process, not just a final result — a process note, sketch log, commit history, or draft trail.
Complete the checklist in this package before submitting.
primary_task: Create the safety or citizenship artifact for this unit using only fictional names, fictional accounts, and invented examples — never real personal information, real screenshots of real accounts, or a real classmate's data.
test_or_check_criteria: Every claim or design choice in the submission can be traced to digital footprints or another named topic from this unit — nothing is left unexplained.
The submission runs, displays, or demonstrates correctly on at least two different sample inputs or scenarios the student chooses.
No real password, API key, account credential, precise location, or other real personal/system data appears anywhere in the submission — fictional or sandbox examples only.
The student can explain, in their own words, why each step or decision was made, not just that it works.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: This project never touches a real account, a real password or API key, a live production system, or another person's real data. Use fictional names, sandbox environments, local files, or already-approved sample data throughout. Submit code, screenshots of your own sandbox, diagrams, or a written walkthrough — a live public deployment is never required.

copyright_and_authorship: The final submitted work must remain your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI assistant may help you plan, explain a concept, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but may not produce the graded work itself. Never request, store, or submit a real password, API key, access token, or other real credential; use only fictional accounts and sandboxed or offline systems.
remediation: If the project stalls, step back to the smallest version of the task: rebuild just the part covering digital footprints in isolation, using a worked example from this unit as a model, then re-attach it to the full project once that smaller piece works and you can explain why.
extension: Once the core project is working, extend it to handle a new constraint or edge case related to evaluating a website for trust, or compare two different approaches to the same problem and explain the real tradeoff between them in your own words.
